passage: In their house in Rewari, Kashish, eighteen, had started doing something strange. Before bed she checked the gas knob, then the front door latch, then the gas again. She had never done that before her brother Sachin came home to study for his civil services prelims. Sachin checked everything twice, sometimes three times, and asked her whether she'd locked the scooter or switched off the geyser, in a tight, fast voice. The whole house had started to hum with it. One night their mother saw Kashish at the gas knob and sat them both down. She said plainly that Sachin was anxious about his exam, that it wasn't anyone's fault, and that there would be one routine now: Ma would lock up at ten, once, and nobody else would check. Sachin agreed to talk to a counsellor. Kashish slept better that week.

qa.a: Ma, once, and nobody else would check.

qa.q: Why had Kashish started checking the gas and the latch?
qa.a: Sachin's tight, repeated questions filled the house with tension, and she picked up his alarm without deciding to.

qa.q: Which choices by their mother lightened the house?
qa.a: Naming Sachin's anxiety honestly and without blame, setting one clear locking routine, and Sachin agreeing to see a counsellor.

qa.q: What was it like for Kashish living with Sachin's worry?
qa.a: The house seemed to hum with tension, and she found herself copying his checking, until the new routine let her sleep better.

passage: In the flat in Johannesburg, Siddiq noticed he'd started checking his phone for university messages every ten minutes, even though his own exams were months away. It had begun when his older brother Thabo's finals started. Thabo paced the kitchen at night, refreshed the results page, and asked Siddiq three times whether he'd set the alarm, whether the lights were off, whether he'd heard anything. The tension crept into Siddiq like cold. One Sunday their father called a family meeting at the kitchen table. "We're all jumpy," he said honestly. "Thabo is stressed, and it's catching." They agreed: dinner at seven, phones in a basket till eight, and Thabo would check the results page only once, in the morning. Siddiq felt his shoulders drop for the first time in weeks.

qa.a: Dinner at seven, phones in a basket till eight, and Thabo checking the results page only once, in the morning.

passage: At the college counselling centre, Jagdish, a first-year, sat twisting his cap. "It's not me who's anxious," he began. "It's my sister Preeti. She's in final year here, placements. She calls me every night, asks if I've locked the room, if I've backed up my files, if I've checked the notice board. Now I do it too. I checked my laptop backup five times yesterday." The counsellor nodded. "Worry can travel through a family, even at a distance. It's nobody's fault." Together they made a plan: one fixed call time with Preeti, eight o'clock, ten minutes; one backup a day, at night; and an honest talk with Preeti about what the calls were doing to him. "Would you like her to come to a session too?" the counsellor asked. Jagdish nodded, relieved.

qa.a: Five times.

qa.q: Why was Jagdish relieved at the end of the session?
qa.a: He learned that the checking he had picked up from his sister was understandable and nobody's fault, and he had a plan that included Preeti.

qa.q: Which parts of the plan could lighten the worry for both siblings?
qa.a: A fixed short call time, one backup a day, and an honest talk with Preeti, possibly in a shared session.

qa.q: How might Preeti feel when she hears what the calls were doing to Jagdish?
qa.a: Preeti may be surprised and sorry, not having realised her worry was spreading, and perhaps relieved to get support too.

You asked about my family, so here's the strange part. The year my sister Afreen did her final year in pharmacy, I was nineteen, and I caught her worry like a cold. passage: In their Mumbai flat, Vasudha had been waiting for placement results for two weeks. She refreshed her email constantly, even at meals. She sighed loudly at every notification. Her younger sister Aditi, in first year, was fine at first. Then Aditi noticed she was refreshing her own email too, though she wasn't waiting for anything. Her heart jumped at every ping. She started biting her nails. One evening she said, "Didi, I think your worry is getting into me." Vasudha looked up, startled, then laughed shakily. "Mine's getting into me too." They talked for a long time on the balcony. Vasudha admitted she was terrified. Aditi admitted she didn't even know what she was scared of. They agreed on a small routine: phones in the basket during dinner, and a walk together after. The next week, Aditi stopped refreshing her email.

I'm Sarita. I never used to check the gas knob. By April I was checking it three times before bed.

It started in March, when Binita didi's final exams began. She'd walk around the flat at night checking the door, the gas, her hall ticket, the alarm. She'd ask me, "Did you lock the balcony?" even when she'd seen me lock it. Her voice was tight all the time.

At first I found it annoying. Then I caught myself doing it too. I began checking my own bag twice for my college ID. I lay awake listening for the door.

One Sunday Mummy sat us both down. She said, "We're all carrying Binita's exam fear. Let's talk about it plainly." Didi admitted she was scared. I admitted I'd started checking too. We made a rule: one check of the gas and the door, by whoever is last to bed, and then we say goodnight. It's lighter now. Mostly.

qa.a: By April Sarita was checking it three times before bed.

qa.q: How did Sarita feel as Binita didi's checking spread through the flat?
qa.a: Sarita first felt annoyed, then uneasy and tense enough to lie awake listening for the door and to start checking things too.

qa.q: Why did Mummy's plain talk and the one-check rule help?
qa.a: Naming the fear let everyone admit it, and a single agreed check gave the house a clear routine instead of endless checking.

qa.a: Binita didi might feel guilty and surprised, but also relieved that the worry was out in the open and shared.

passage:
Counsellor's note, college wellbeing centre

Tanvir, first year, came in today saying he couldn't focus in lectures. As we talked, it emerged that his older brother is preparing for a competitive exam at home and has been very anxious for months: counting study hours aloud, checking the time every few minutes, asking the family to keep phones silent.

Tanvir now does similar things. He showed me his planner with every half hour marked, and said he checks his watch "maybe fifty times a class". He said he felt jumpy at home and felt he wasn't allowed to relax while his brother suffered.

We talked about how worry can travel through a house without anyone meaning it to. I suggested he try saying to his brother, gently, how the tension feels to him, and that the family agree on shared quiet hours and some shared non-study time.

He'll come back next week. I'll follow up.

In their small house in Latur, Charu was preparing for the bank exam, and everyone could feel it. She checked the alarm twice every night, asked their mother three times whether the gas was off, and jumped at every phone ring.
Her younger sister Kalyani, eighteen and in first-year BCom, had always been easygoing. But lately she caught herself checking the door latch twice, then three times. She packed her college bag, unpacked it, packed it again. Her stomach was tight before every class, though nothing was wrong.
One evening, their mother noticed Kalyani at the latch. "You too?"
Kalyani laughed nervously. "I don't know when I started."
That night their mother sat both girls down. "Charu, the exam is hard, and it's okay to be worried. Kalyani, you don't have to carry her worry." She set a rule: one check of the house at ten, done by her. Then lights out.
Charu looked at her sister, surprised. "I didn't know it was affecting you."

In their flat in Lagos, Chidi's older brother Daniel was in his final engineering year, and his worry filled every room. He checked the stove before bed, then again. He asked Chidi each morning whether the back door was locked. When the power flickered, he unplugged everything.
Chidi, nineteen and in first year, used to tease him. But this term Chidi noticed a change. Walking to lectures, Chidi's hand kept going to the pocket, checking for keys. At night Chidi got up to look at the stove, even after Daniel had checked.
One Sunday, Chidi said it straight out. "Daniel, I think your worry is rubbing off on me. I check things now. I never used to."
Daniel sat down heavily. "I didn't want that."
"I know."
They agreed on a simple plan: one check of the flat at ten, taking turns, written on a card by the door. Daniel also said he'd talk to someone at the student centre about his stress. The card went up that night.
